name: Pakistan
governanceModel: Aspirational, adoption-led National AI Policy 2025 led by the Ministry of IT & Telecommunication, with data-protection legislation still pending
debateTopics: Ambitious AI targets vs. limited compute and funding

overview:
Pakistan's AI approach is set out in its National AI Policy 2025, approved by the Federal Cabinet in late July 2025 and led by the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) under Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja. The policy is aspirational and adoption-led rather than restrictive: a six-pillar framework spanning AI innovation, public awareness, secure and responsible systems, sectoral transformation, infrastructure, and international partnerships, backed by headline targets such as training one million people in AI by 2030, thousands of annual scholarships and internships, and proposed AI Innovation and Venture funds.

Implementation is being built out through a National AI Council, a Policy Implementation Cell and Centres of Excellence in AI, and the government has signalled larger ambitions — at the Indus AI Summit in Islamabad (February 2026) the Prime Minister announced a plan to invest around US$1 billion in AI by 2030. The economic backdrop is a fast-growing IT-export and freelancer sector, with IT exports reaching a record US$4.6bn in FY2026. Yet the enabling environment remains thin: domestic compute is nascent (a handful of academic supercomputers rather than frontier-scale clusters), and Pakistan still lacks a comprehensive data-protection law, with a Personal Data Protection Bill pending for years. Governance is therefore more a statement of intent than a binding regime as of mid-2026.

currentDirection.summary: Pakistan's direction is one of gradual institution-building on an adoption-first policy: the National AI Policy 2025 and the emerging AI Council set intent and targets, and the government has floated larger investment, but binding regulation is limited and a data-protection law remains pending. The trajectory is expansion of ambition rather than a tightening or loosening of rules.

recentDevelopments.text: At the Indus AI Summit in Islamabad (9–10 February 2026), Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced plans to invest around US$1bn in AI by 2030, alongside 1,000 AI PhD scholarships and a national programme to train one million AI specialists.

MoITT began formally notifying the National AI Council to provide strategic oversight of the National AI Policy 2025, supported by a Policy Implementation Cell and Centres of Excellence in AI in major cities.

Pakistan's IT exports reached a record US$4.6bn in FY2026 (up roughly 21% year on year), with freelancer remittances rising sharply — underlining an IT-services and freelance economy that AI is reshaping.

The Federal Cabinet approved the National AI Policy 2025 (late July 2025), a six-pillar framework covering innovation, awareness, secure systems, sectoral transformation, infrastructure and international partnerships, with a headline goal of training one million people in AI by 2030.

Reporting indicated Pakistan still lacks a comprehensive data-protection law: the Personal Data Protection Bill remains pending before Parliament, while the Prevention of Electronic Crimes (Amendment) Act 2025 tightened content and cybercrime rules — leaving a notable governance gap for AI systems that process personal data.

Pakistan's AI research base remained concentrated in academia — notably NUST (home to the National Centre of Artificial Intelligence and the fastest supercomputer in Pakistani academia, at roughly petaflop scale) and LUMS — rather than in frontier industrial labs.

policyAndRegulation.title: National AI Policy 2025
policyAndRegulation.summary: Approved by the Federal Cabinet in late July 2025 and led by MoITT, this is Pakistan's foundational AI policy — a six-pillar framework (AI innovation; public awareness; secure and responsible systems; sectoral transformation; infrastructure; international partnerships). It sets adoption and skills targets (e.g. one million people trained by 2030, thousands of annual scholarships and internships, compute access for 150 institutions) and proposes AI Innovation and AI Venture funds, overseen by a National AI Council. It is a policy framework rather than binding legislation.

policyAndRegulation.title: Personal Data Protection Bill
policyAndRegulation.summary: A draft Personal Data Protection Bill has been introduced by MoITT and revised over several years but not enacted; as of mid-2026 Pakistan has no comprehensive data-protection statute. Its absence is widely flagged as a gap for AI governance, given how much AI depends on personal-data processing.

policyAndRegulation.title: Prevention of Electronic Crimes (Amendment) Act 2025 (PECA Amendment)
policyAndRegulation.summary: An amendment to Pakistan's cybercrime law passed in 2025, tightening rules on online content and electronic offences. While not AI-specific, it forms part of the digital-governance backdrop against which AI content and platforms operate, and has drawn civil-society concern over free-expression effects.

researchEcosystem.summary: Pakistan's AI research is concentrated in a handful of universities — most prominently NUST (via SEECS and the National Centre of Artificial Intelligence, which runs labs across several universities) and LUMS — supported by modest academic high-performance computing rather than frontier-scale clusters. The wider ecosystem leans heavily on a large, export-oriented IT-services and freelancer base applying AI tools, rather than on domestic foundation-model development.

notableGaps.note: Pakistan has no comprehensive data-protection statute in force as of mid-2026; the Personal Data Protection Bill has been pending for years. This leaves AI systems that process personal data without a clear statutory baseline.

Domestic compute is nascent — a few academic supercomputers rather than frontier-scale clusters — and fiscal and foreign-exchange constraints put the policy's headline targets (one million trained, ~US$1bn investment) at risk of outrunning delivery. Several such figures are announced ambitions rather than confirmed spending.
There is no domestic frontier or near-frontier model developer; Pakistan's AI strength is an applied, export-oriented IT-services and freelancer economy rather than foundation-model training.

debates.topic: Ambitious AI targets vs. limited compute and funding
debates.summary: Pakistan's AI policy sets striking targets — one million trained by 2030, thousands of scholarships, ~US$1bn of investment — against a backdrop of nascent compute and tight public finances, raising questions about deliverability.
debates.expanded: The National AI Policy 2025 and subsequent announcements are heavy on ambition: mass skilling, Centres of Excellence, innovation and venture funds, and a national compute grid. But domestic compute today amounts to a few academic supercomputers, and Pakistan's fiscal position and foreign-exchange constraints make large GPU procurement and sustained funding hard. Supporters argue bold targets mobilise attention and partners; sceptics warn of a gap between announced figures and actual delivery, and note that much of the headline investment remains aspirational.

debates.topic: Regulating AI without a data-protection law
debates.summary: Pakistan is promoting AI adoption while lacking a comprehensive data-protection statute, leaving a governance gap for systems that rely on large-scale personal-data processing.
debates.expanded: The National AI Policy speaks of secure and responsible systems, but the Personal Data Protection Bill remains unpassed, and the main recent legislative movement — the PECA Amendment 2025 — is a cybercrime/content measure that civil-society groups argue tilts toward control rather than rights protection. The debate is whether Pakistan can build trustworthy AI adoption without first establishing baseline privacy protections, and how to sequence enabling policy against overdue data-protection legislation.

debates.topic: An IT-export and freelancer economy meeting AI
debates.summary: With record IT exports and a vast freelancer base, Pakistan sees AI as both an opportunity to move up the value chain and a threat to commoditised services work.
debates.expanded: Pakistan's IT exports hit a record US$4.6bn in FY2026, and freelancing is a major source of foreign earnings. AI could let Pakistani firms and freelancers offer higher-value services, but it also risks automating exactly the kind of commoditised outsourcing work many rely on. Policymakers frame skilling and adoption as the response; the open question is whether Pakistan can reskill fast enough to capture AI's upside rather than be squeezed by it.
